questions.question: The best description of the effect of a catalyst on a chemical reaction is that it
questions.answer: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. It lowers the activation energy of both the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, so both rates increase equally and the position of equilibrium is unchanged (B).
options: increases the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount.
lowers the activation energy of both the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount.
lowers the activation energy of the forward reaction and raises the activation energy of the reverse reaction.
lowers the activation energy of the reverse reaction without changing the activation energy of the forward reaction.

questions.question: Methanoic acid and ethanoic acid are both weak acids with the following acid dissociation constants $K_a$ at $25^\circ$C: methanoic acid (HCOOH) $=1.82\times10^{-4}$; ethanoic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$) $=1.74\times10^{-5}$. Two separate solutions were prepared, one of $0.1$ M methanoic acid and the other of $0.1$ M ethanoic acid. Which one of the following would be present in the lowest concentration at $25^\circ$C?
questions.answer: Both acids are weak, so most of each remains un-ionised (A and C are about $0.1$ M). $[\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-]\approx\sqrt{1.74\times10^{-5}\times0.1}=1.3\times10^{-3}$ M, and $[\text{HCOO}^-]\approx\sqrt{1.82\times10^{-4}\times0.1}=4.3\times10^{-3}$ M. The lowest is $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ in the ethanoic acid solution (B).
options: HCOOH in the methanoic acid solution

questions.question:
Some solid copper sulfate crystals were added to a beaker of water, stirred to dissolve the solid, covered to prevent evaporation and left to stand. After 1 day, solid crystals were still present in the beaker. More solid copper sulfate, which contained radioactive atoms, was then added to the beaker. The beaker was then covered and left to stand for a second day. Assume that temperature has remained constant. Which of the following statements is/are correct after the 2-day period?

I – the solution will contain radioactive atoms as some of the radioactive solid will have dissolved.
II – there will be more solid remaining in the beaker than was present before the radioactive solid was added.
III – the final solution of copper sulfate will be more concentrated than it was after 1 day.
questions.answer: The saturated solution is in dynamic equilibrium, so dissolving and crystallising continue and radioactive atoms enter the solution (I true). Extra solid was added to an already saturated solution, so more solid remains (II true). At constant temperature the saturated solution has the same concentration (III false). So I and II only (C).

questions.question: A sample of an unknown solution is tested with the indicator bromothymol blue. The solution turns yellow on the addition of this indicator. What would the solution be?
questions.answer: Bromothymol blue is yellow in acidic solution. $\text{NH}_4^+$ is a weak acid, so $\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$ is acidic (D). $\text{CH}_3\text{COOK}$ is basic, and LiCl and $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$ are neutral.

questions.question: When two moles of an organic compound are burnt in oxygen, eight moles of carbon dioxide gas are formed. In a second test, when a few drops of bromine are added to the compound and shaken, the bromine rapidly decolourises. The formula of the compound could be
questions.answer: Each mole of the compound gives 4 mol of $\text{CO}_2$, so it has 4 carbons (eliminates C and D). Bromine rapidly decolourises, so it is unsaturated (an alkene, $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}$), so it is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ (A).

questions.question: The molecule $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ (molar mass $=104$ g mol$^{-1}$) forms a condensation polymer in which the average polymer molecule contains 1000 monomer units. The approximate molar mass of the polymer, in g mol$^{-1}$, is
questions.answer: Joining 1000 monomers forms 999 ester links, each releasing one $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ($18$ g mol$^{-1}$): $M=1000\times104-999\times18=86\,000$ g mol$^{-1}$ (B).

questions.question: Which of the following solutions, upon mixing, will produce the solution with the highest temperature change?
questions.answer: The temperature change is proportional to (moles of water formed) / (total volume). A: $0.0025$ mol in $150$ mL. B: $0.001$ mol in $300$ mL. C: $n(\text{H}^+)=0.020$ and $n(\text{OH}^-)=0.020$, so $0.020$ mol in $150$ mL. D: $0.005$ mol in $150$ mL. C produces the most heat per volume (C).
options: $50$ mL of $0.050$ M $\text{HNO}_3$ + $100$ mL of $0.4$ M NaOH
$200$ mL of $0.05$ M $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ + $100$ mL of $0.01$ M NaOH
$100$ mL of $0.1$ M $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ + $50$ mL of $0.4$ M KOH
$50$ mL of $0.2$ M HCl + $100$ mL of $0.025$ M $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$

questions.question: Which of the following is not an amphiprotic species?
questions.answer: An amphiprotic species can both donate and accept a proton. $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ has no hydrogen to donate, so it can only act as a base (B).

questions.question: What are the two Brønsted–Lowry acids in the following reaction? $$\text{HNO}_2(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{NO}_2^-(aq)$$
questions.answer: In the forward reaction $\text{HNO}_2$ donates a proton (acid) to $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (base). In the reverse reaction $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ donates a proton (acid) to $\text{NO}_2^-$ (base). The acids are $\text{HNO}_2$ and $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ (A).

questions.question: Which of the following compounds is the most basic?
questions.answer: The amine has a lone pair on nitrogen that readily accepts a proton, making it the most basic. The amide's lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl, and the alcohol and ester are not basic (B).

questions.question: Limestone ($\text{CaCO}_3$) can be eroded by acids. What volume (in mL) of $11.5$ mol L$^{-1}$ nitric acid ($\text{HNO}_3$) is required for complete reaction with $24.7$ g of limestone?
questions.answer: $n(\text{CaCO}_3)=\dfrac{24.7}{100.09}=0.2468$ mol. $\text{CaCO}_3+2\text{HNO}_3\rightarrow\text{Ca(NO}_3)_2+\text{H}_2\text{O}+\text{CO}_2$, so $n(\text{HNO}_3)=0.4935$ mol and $V=\dfrac{0.4935}{11.5}=0.0429$ L $=42.9$ mL (A).

questions.question: Which of the following changes takes place when 500 mL of water is added to 500 mL of 1 mol/L acetic acid?
questions.answer: Dilution lowers $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$, so the pH increases. For a weak acid, dilution shifts the equilibrium $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ towards the side with more particles, so the percentage ionisation increases (A).
options: pH increases, percentage ionisation does not change
pH decreases, percentage ionisation does not change

questions.question: A solution is prepared by mixing $100.0$ mL of $0.1$ mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{NaNO}_3$ with $200.0$ mL of $0.100$ mol L$^{-1}$ HCl and then adding sufficient water to give it a final volume of $500$ mL. What is the pH of the solution?
questions.answer: $\text{NaNO}_3$ does not affect the pH. $n(\text{HCl})=0.100\times0.2000=0.0200$ mol in $0.500$ L, so $[\text{H}^+]=0.0400$ mol L$^{-1}$ and $\text{pH}=1.40$ (C).

questions.question: At $25^\circ$C, solutions of barium ions ($\text{Ba}^{2+}$) and hydroxide ions ($\text{OH}^-$) are mixed so that the following concentrations are initially present: $[\text{Ba}^{2+}]=0.030$ M and $[\text{OH}^-]=0.065$ M. Which of the following identifies the correct ionic product and whether precipitation occurs for this reaction?
questions.answer:
$Q=[\text{Ba}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2=0.030\times(0.065)^2=1.27\times10^{-4}$. The $K_{sp}$ of $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is about $5\times10^{-3}$ (a soluble hydroxide), so $Q<K_{sp}$ and no precipitate forms (C).
*(The school's key gives A (Yes), but $Q$ is well below the $K_{sp}$ of $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$, so no precipitation occurs.)*

questions.question: The data sheet lists the $K_{sp}$ value for lead iodide, $\text{PbI}_2$, as $9.8\times10^{-9}$. If the concentration of lead ions in a sample solution is $5.0\times10^{-5}$ mol L$^{-1}$, then what is the maximum concentration of iodide ions in the same solution?

Three gases L, M and N in a sealed $5.0$ L container react to form an equilibrium. The graph shows how the concentration of these gases changes at time $t_1$ when the mixture is heated. Which is correct of the reaction in this graph?
questions.answer: On heating, $[\text{M}]$ falls by about $0.4$, $[\text{N}]$ falls by about $0.2$ and $[\text{L}]$ rises by about $0.2$, so L is on one side with M and N on the other, in the ratio $\text{L}:\text{M}:\text{N}=1:2:1$: $\text{L}\rightleftharpoons2\text{M}+\text{N}$. Heating shifted the equilibrium to the left (towards L), which favours the endothermic direction, so the reverse is endothermic and the forward reaction is exothermic (A).
options: $\text{L}(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{M}(g)+\text{N}(g)$ and the forward reaction is exothermic
$2\text{M}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{L}(g)+\text{N}(g)$ and the forward reaction is endothermic
$2\text{M}(g)+\text{N}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{L}(g)$ and the forward reaction is exothermic
$\text{L}(g)+2\text{M}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{N}(g)$ and the forward reaction is endothermic

questions.question: The organic compound ethylene ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$) can be reacted with water to make ethanol: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$. A reaction uses $18.4$ g of ethylene but only produces $27.6$ g of ethanol at the end of the reaction pathway. What is the percentage yield for this reaction?
questions.answer: $n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4)=\dfrac{18.4}{28.05}=0.656$ mol, so the theoretical yield of ethanol is $0.656\times46.07=30.2$ g. Percentage yield $=\dfrac{27.6}{30.2}\times100=91\%$ (D).

questions.question: This conductivity graph (conductance against mL of strong base added) represents a reaction between two reactants. What are the two reactants?
questions.answer: The base added is strong, so A is excluded (ammonia is weak). A strong acid with a strong base would show a sharp V-shaped graph, with a steep fall in conductance as the highly conducting $\text{H}^+$ is removed, and polyprotic $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ would show several changes in slope. The smooth, shallow decrease followed by a steep rise after the equivalence point is the pattern for a weak acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, with a strong base, KOH (D).

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of compounds are NOT isomers?
questions.answer: Butane is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$ and cyclobutane is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$, so they have different molecular formulae and are not isomers (C). The other pairs are $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$ and $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}$ respectively.

questions.question:
The following table shows the value of the ionisation constant of pure water at various temperatures and at a constant pressure.

| Temperature of water ($^\circ$C) | 0 | 25 | 50 | 75 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_w$ | $1.1\times10^{-15}$ | $1.0\times10^{-14}$ | $5.5\times10^{-14}$ | $2.0\times10^{-13}$ |

Given this data, which one of the following statements about pure water is correct?
questions.answer: $K_w$ increases with temperature. In pure water $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=[\text{OH}^-]=\sqrt{K_w}$, so both increase and the pH falls. The pH is 7 only at $25^\circ$C (B).
options: The $[\text{OH}^-]$ will decrease with increasing temperature
The $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ will increase with increasing temperature
Its pH will increase with increasing temperature.
Its pH will always be exactly 7 at any temperature.

questions.question: Carbon monoxide and hydrogen can be produced from the reaction of methane with steam: $\text{CH}_4(g)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}(g)+3\text{H}_2(g)$, $\Delta H=+206$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Some methane and steam were placed in a closed container and allowed to react at a fixed temperature. The graph shows the changes in concentration of methane and carbon monoxide as the reaction progresses. On the graph, draw a line to predict the change in concentration of hydrogen gas as the reaction progresses. Label this line. Explain why you have drawn the line in this position.
questions.answer: The $\text{H}_2$ line starts at zero and rises, levelling off at the same time as the CO and $\text{CH}_4$ lines (when equilibrium is reached). Its final height is three times that of the CO line, since the equation shows 3 mol of $\text{H}_2$ formed for every 1 mol of CO formed, so $[\text{H}_2]=3[\text{CO}]$ at all times.

questions.question: For the equilibrium $\text{CH}_4(g)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}(g)+3\text{H}_2(g)$ ($\Delta H=+206$ kJ mol$^{-1}$), the graph shows how the concentrations of methane and carbon monoxide change over time in the absence of a catalyst. On the graph, draw a line to show how the formation of carbon monoxide would differ over time in the presence of a catalyst. Label this line. Explain why you have drawn the line in this position.
questions.answer: The catalysed line starts at zero and is steeper, so it levels off sooner, but at the same final height as the uncatalysed CO line. A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful and the rate of reaction increases. It speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the same equilibrium position (and the same amount of CO) is reached, only faster.

questions.question: Lead(II) chloride is sparingly soluble in water, and this equilibrium is set up between the solid and its ions in solution. Given its $K_{sp}=1.7\times10^{-5}$, determine the solubility of lead(II) chloride.
questions.answer:
$\text{PbCl}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Pb}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{Cl}^-(aq)$. Let the solubility be $s$: $[\text{Pb}^{2+}]=s$, $[\text{Cl}^-]=2s$.
$K_{sp}=s(2s)^2=4s^3=1.7\times10^{-5}$, so $s^3=4.25\times10^{-6}$ and $s=1.6\times10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Calculate and compare the solubility of lead(II) chloride ($K_{sp}=1.7\times10^{-5}$) when dissolved in $0.35$ mol L$^{-1}$ NaCl.
questions.answer:
$[\text{Cl}^-]=0.35+2s\approx0.35$ mol L$^{-1}$ (the $2s$ is negligible).
$K_{sp}=s(0.35)^2=1.7\times10^{-5}$, so $s=\dfrac{1.7\times10^{-5}}{0.1225}=1.39\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$.
$\text{PbCl}_2$ is about $115$ times less soluble in $0.35$ M NaCl than in pure water ($1.6\times10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$), because of the common ion effect: the extra $\text{Cl}^-$ shifts the equilibrium towards the solid.

questions.question: Using IUPAC nomenclature, name the compounds shown (Compound 1: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$; Compound 2: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$; Compound 3: $\text{HCOOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$).
questions.answer:
- Compound 1: **propanamide**
- Compound 2: **2,3-dimethylpentane**
- Compound 3: **propyl methanoate** (the alcohol part is named first; the acid chain comes from the side with the C=O)
*(The school writes "1-propyl methanoate"; the locant is not needed.)*

questions.question: Compare the intermolecular forces in the molecules propanamide ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$), 2,3-dimethylpentane and propyl methanoate ($\text{HCOOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$), and predict the order of boiling points (lowest to highest) of these molecules. Explain your prediction.
questions.answer:
**Order of increasing boiling point: 2,3-dimethylpentane < propyl methanoate < propanamide.**

The stronger the intermolecular forces, the more energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the higher the boiling point.
- **2,3-Dimethylpentane** is a non-polar alkane. It has only weak dispersion forces .
- **Propyl methanoate** is an ester, which is polar, so it has dipole–dipole forces as well as dispersion forces, but no hydrogen bonding between its molecules.
- **Propanamide** is polar and has an N–H group, so it forms strong hydrogen bonds between molecules (to the C=O oxygen and between N–H groups), more than one per molecule, in addition to dipole–dipole and dispersion forces.
*(In practice the boiling points are about $90^\circ$C for 2,3-dimethylpentane and $81^\circ$C for propyl methanoate because dispersion forces increase with molar mass, but the intended prediction by type of intermolecular force is as above.)*

questions.question: The table shows acid dissociation constants at $25^\circ$C: nitrous acid $\text{HNO}_2$, $7.2\times10^{-4}$; hydrofluoric acid HF, $6.6\times10^{-4}$; hydrocyanic acid HCN, $6.2\times10^{-10}$; propanoic acid $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, $1.34\times10^{-5}$; chlorous acid $\text{HClO}_2$, $1.1\times10^{-2}$. Identify the weakest acid in the table and determine the $\text{p}K_a$ value for this acid at $25^\circ$C.
questions.answer: The weakest acid has the smallest $K_a$: **hydrocyanic acid**. $\text{p}K_a=-\log(6.2\times10^{-10})=9.21$.

questions.question: The table shows acid dissociation constants at $25^\circ$C: $\text{HNO}_2$, $7.2\times10^{-4}$; HF, $6.6\times10^{-4}$; HCN, $6.2\times10^{-10}$; $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, $1.34\times10^{-5}$; $\text{HClO}_2$, $1.1\times10^{-2}$. Identify the weakest base formed from these acids. What is the $\text{p}K_b$ for this base at $25^\circ$C?
questions.answer:
The strongest acid forms the weakest conjugate base. $\text{HClO}_2$ is the strongest acid, so the weakest base is the chlorite ion, $\text{ClO}_2^-$.
$\text{p}K_a=-\log(1.1\times10^{-2})=1.96$, so $\text{p}K_b=14.00-1.96=12.04$.

questions.question: Calculate the pH of a $0.010$ M solution of propanoic acid ($K_a=1.34\times10^{-5}$) at $25^\circ$C.
questions.answer:
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$.
$K_a=\dfrac{x^2}{0.010-x}\approx\dfrac{x^2}{0.010}=1.34\times10^{-5}$, so $x^2=1.34\times10^{-7}$ and $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=3.66\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$.
$\text{pH}=-\log(3.66\times10^{-4})=3.44$.

questions.question: A buffer solution is prepared by combining $100$ mL of $0.010$ M nitrous acid ($K_a=7.2\times10^{-4}$) and $80$ mL of $0.010$ M $\text{NaNO}_2$. Calculate the pH of this buffer solution and explain the classification of the solution as a buffer.
questions.answer:
After mixing (total volume $180$ mL): $[\text{HNO}_2]=0.010\times\dfrac{100}{180}=5.56\times10^{-3}$ M and $[\text{NO}_2^-]=0.010\times\dfrac{80}{180}=4.44\times10^{-3}$ M.
$K_a=\dfrac{[\text{NO}_2^-][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]}{[\text{HNO}_2]}$. Let $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=x$:
$$7.2\times10^{-4}=\frac{(4.44\times10^{-3}+x)\,x}{5.56\times10^{-3}-x}$$
The approximation that $x$ is negligible is not valid here, since $K_a$ is relatively large. Solving the quadratic $x^2+5.16\times10^{-3}x-4.0\times10^{-6}=0$ gives $x=6.8\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$, so $\text{pH}=3.17$.
*(Using the approximation $x\ll$ the concentrations, as the school does, gives $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=9.0\times10^{-4}$ and $\text{pH}=3.05$; this is accepted for the marks but is less accurate.)*
**Buffer:** the solution contains a weak acid ($\text{HNO}_2$) and its conjugate base ($\text{NO}_2^-$) in comparable concentrations. If a small amount of acid is added, $\text{NO}_2^-$ reacts with the $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$; if base is added, $\text{HNO}_2$ reacts with the $\text{OH}^-$. By Le Chatelier's principle the ratio $[\text{HNO}_2]/[\text{NO}_2^-]$ changes only slightly, so the pH stays almost constant.

questions.question: A student conducts an investigation to measure the enthalpy of neutralisation using a polystyrene cup calorimeter with a lid and thermometer (see diagram). The reaction mixture consisted of $50.0$ mL of diluted potassium hydroxide solution and $50.0$ mL of a $1.5$ mol L$^{-1}$ solution of nitric acid. The student noticed that the temperature rose from $23^\circ$C to a maximum of $32^\circ$C. Determine the enthalpy of neutralisation for this reaction.
questions.answer:
$\text{KOH}(aq)+\text{HNO}_3(aq)\rightarrow\text{KNO}_3(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$
$\Delta T=32-23=9^\circ$C. Taking the solution as $100$ g with $c=4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$:
$q=mc\Delta T=100\times4.18\times9=3762$ J $=3.762$ kJ.
$n(\text{HNO}_3)=1.5\times0.0500=0.075$ mol, so $n(\text{H}_2\text{O})=0.075$ mol (1:1 ratio, taking the nitric acid as the reagent that is completely used).
$$\Delta H=-\frac{3.762}{0.075}=-50.2\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
*(This assumes that all the acid reacts, i.e. the KOH is not the limiting reagent, as in the school's answer.)*

questions.question: Compounds A and B are isomers with the molecular formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{Cl}$. Samples of compounds A and B are heated separately with sodium hydroxide to produce compounds C and D respectively. A student used samples of compound C in a series of reactions to produce propyl propanoate, a volatile compound with a strong, pungent but sweet pineapple-like smell. Identify all compounds and construct a flow chart to outline a series of reactions that the student could use to produce propyl propanoate using compound C. In your flow chart identify the types of reactions that are carried out and the reagents required for each step.
questions.answer:
- **A** is 1-chloropropane and **B** is 2-chloropropane (the two isomers of $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{Cl}$).
- Heating with NaOH is a **substitution** reaction: A gives **C, propan-1-ol**, and B gives **D, propan-2-ol** (with NaCl).
- Flow chart from C: propan-1-ol $\xrightarrow{\text{oxidation, } \text{H}^+/\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-},\text{ heat}}$ propanoic acid; then propanoic acid + propan-1-ol (compound C) $\xrightarrow{\text{esterification (condensation), conc. }\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{, heat under reflux}}$ **propyl propanoate**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (+ $\text{H}_2\text{O}$).

questions.question: Propyl propanoate is made from propan-1-ol (compound C) and another compound. Draw the structural formula of the compound that reacted with compound C to produce propyl propanoate. What qualitative results would identify that the reaction from compound C to synthesise that which you have drawn has occurred?
questions.answer:
The compound is **propanoic acid**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ (drawn with $\text{CH}_3\text{–CH}_2\text{–C(=O)–OH}$).
It is made by oxidising propan-1-ol with acidified dichromate: the solution changes colour from **orange to green** ($\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\rightarrow\text{Cr}^{3+}$). (Acidified permanganate would change from purple to colourless.)

questions.question: Identify ONE risk associated with carrying out the reaction that formed propyl propanoate (esterification of propanoic acid with propan-1-ol using concentrated sulfuric acid) in a school laboratory and state how this risk can be minimised.
questions.answer:
Any one of:
- Concentrated sulfuric acid is corrosive: wear safety glasses, gloves and a lab coat, and add the acid slowly and carefully (in a fume cupboard if possible).
- The alcohol and ester are flammable and volatile: heat with a hot water bath (not a naked flame) and use a condenser (reflux) so vapours are not released.

questions.question: Outline the use of solubility equilibria by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples when removing toxicity from foods.
questions.answer: Some foods, such as cycad fruit, contain toxins that dissolve in water: toxin(s) $\rightleftharpoons$ toxin(aq). The food is cut or ground up and soaked or leached in running water (a stream) or rinsed repeatedly. The dissolved toxins are carried away, lowering their concentration in the water. By Le Châtelier's principle the equilibrium shifts to the right, dissolving more toxin from the food. Repeated soaking and rinsing over time lowers the toxin content until the food is safe to eat.

questions.question: Three $25.00$ mL samples of a $0.1034$ mol L$^{-1}$ solution of oxalic acid were titrated to standardise a NaOH solution according to $\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4(aq)+2\text{NaOH}(aq)\rightarrow\text{Na}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4(aq)+2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$. The average volume required for neutralisation was $25.75$ mL. Calculate the molarity of the NaOH solution.

Four flasks were each prepared with a mixture of $25$ mL of water and $10$ mL of ethanol. Two aspirin tablets ($\text{C}_9\text{H}_8\text{O}_4$) were dissolved in each flask and titrated with the standardised NaOH solution ($0.2008$ mol L$^{-1}$) according to $\text{C}_9\text{H}_8\text{O}_4(aq)+\text{NaOH}(aq)\rightarrow\text{C}_9\text{H}_7\text{O}_4\text{Na}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$. The titration volumes were: trial 1, $16.55$ mL; trial 2, $16.75$ mL; trial 3, $16.60$ mL; trial 4, $16.50$ mL. The packaging claims the tablets contain $350$ mg of aspirin per tablet. Calculate the mass (mg) of aspirin per tablet, and justify whether the claim is true.
questions.answer:
Trial 2 ($16.75$ mL) is an outlier, so the average of the concordant titres is $\dfrac{16.55+16.60+16.50}{3}=16.55$ mL.
$n(\text{NaOH})=0.2008\times0.01655=3.323\times10^{-3}$ mol $=n(\text{aspirin})$ (1:1 ratio).
$m=3.323\times10^{-3}\times180.15=0.5986$ g $=598.6$ mg for two tablets, so **$299.3$ mg per tablet**.
This is less than the claimed $350$ mg (about $14\%$ lower), so the claim is false.

questions.question: A graph of the rate of reaction versus time for a particular chemical reaction is shown. At time $t_1$ the reactant concentration is increased. Account for the shape of the graphs between $t_0$ and $t_1$ and between $t_1$ and $t_2$ in terms of collision theory.
questions.answer:
**$t_0$ to $t_1$:** at $t_0$ only reactants are present at their highest concentration, so the frequency of successful collisions, and hence the forward rate, is highest, while the reverse rate is zero (no products). As the reaction proceeds, reactants are used up, so the forward rate falls; products form, so the reverse rate rises. The rates become equal at equilibrium and stay constant.
**$t_1$ to $t_2$:** adding reactant increases its concentration, so there are more particles per unit volume, more successful collisions per second, and the forward rate increases suddenly (a spike), while the reverse rate is initially unchanged. The forward rate then falls as reactants are used up, and the reverse rate rises as more products form, until the rates are equal again at $t_2$. Both rates are higher than before because the concentrations of reactants and products are higher.

questions.question: With the use of at least ONE diagram, explain the action of soaps in emulsifying oils.
questions.answer:
A soap is the sodium salt of a long-chain fatty acid, e.g. $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_{16}\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$. The anion has a charged, polar, hydrophilic carboxylate head (soluble in water) and a long non-polar hydrocarbon tail, which is hydrophobic (soluble in oil).
In a water–oil mixture the soap anions surround the oil with their tails in the oil and their heads in the water. Agitation breaks the oil into droplets, each surrounded by soap anions, forming **micelles**. The negative charges on the outside of each micelle repel other micelles, so the oil droplets stay dispersed (emulsified) in the water and can be washed away.

questions.question: Initially a $2.00$ L glass vessel contains a mixture of $1.00$ mol of hydrogen gas and $1.00$ mol of iodine gas. The gases react as follows: $\text{H}_2(g)+\text{I}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{HI}(g)$. At $400^\circ$C equilibrium is achieved and the concentration of hydrogen iodide gas is $0.760$ mol L$^{-1}$. Calculate the equilibrium constant for this reaction and discuss what the value indicates about the reaction. Show all working.
questions.answer:
Initial: $[\text{H}_2]=[\text{I}_2]=\dfrac{1.00}{2.00}=0.500$ mol L$^{-1}$, $[\text{HI}]=0$.
Change: $[\text{HI}]$ rises by $0.760$, so $[\text{H}_2]$ and $[\text{I}_2]$ each fall by $0.380$. Equilibrium: $[\text{H}_2]=[\text{I}_2]=0.120$ mol L$^{-1}$.
$$K_{eq}=\frac{[\text{HI}]^2}{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]}=\frac{(0.760)^2}{(0.120)(0.120)}=40.1$$
The value is moderately large ($>1$), so the equilibrium lies to the right and the products are favoured, but the reaction does not go to completion.

questions.question: A solution is thought to contain sodium salts of hydroxide, chloride and sulfate ions. Using only test solutions of $\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2$, $\text{Pb(NO}_3)_2$ and $\text{Mg(NO}_3)_2$, suggest a procedure that could be used to identify and extract each anion. Include expected observations and a balanced chemical equation in your answer.
questions.answer:
Add the cations in an order such that each precipitates only one anion, filtering off each precipitate before the next addition:
1. Add excess $\text{Mg(NO}_3)_2$: a **white precipitate** of $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ shows hydroxide. Filter it off. ($\text{Mg}^{2+}$ does not precipitate chloride or sulfate.)
2. To the filtrate add excess $\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2$: a **white precipitate** of $\text{BaSO}_4$ shows sulfate. Filter it off.
3. To the filtrate add excess $\text{Pb(NO}_3)_2$ last: a **white precipitate** of $\text{PbCl}_2$ shows chloride. Filter it off.
$\text{Pb}^{2+}$ must be added last because it would precipitate sulfate (and hydroxide) as well as chloride. Mg and Ba may be added in either order.
Equations: $\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s)$; $\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq)+\text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)\rightarrow\text{BaSO}_4(s)$; $\text{Pb}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{Cl}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{PbCl}_2(s)$.

questions.question: The diagram shows the structure of the condensation polymer nylon-6,6. Explain what is meant by a 'condensation polymer'.
questions.answer: A condensation polymer forms when monomers with two functional groups react together, with the functional groups joining (here, amide links) and a small molecule (usually water) eliminated for each link formed.

questions.question: Contrast the process of condensation polymerisation with that of addition polymerisation.
questions.answer:
- Addition polymerisation: the C=C double bond in each monomer opens and the monomers join. No atoms are lost, so the polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer.
- Condensation polymerisation: functional groups on different monomers react, joining the monomers, and a small molecule (e.g. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ or HCl) is eliminated. The monomers do not need a double bond, but need two functional groups.

questions.question:
Heptane is a clear, odourless liquid hydrocarbon. Its high flammability gives it properties necessary in many industries, including use as a fuel.

| Species | $\text{O}_2(g)$ | $\text{CO}_2(g)$ | $\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$ | $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{16}(l)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Enthalpy of formation (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | 0 | $-393$ | $-285$ | $-224$ |
| Entropy (J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$) | $+205$ | $+214$ | $+70$ | $+329$ |

Use the data in the table to determine whether the combustion of heptane at 298 K is spontaneous.
questions.answer:
$\text{C}_7\text{H}_{16}(l)+11\text{O}_2(g)\rightarrow7\text{CO}_2(g)+8\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$
$\Delta H=[7(-393)+8(-285)]-[-224+0]=-5031+224=-4807$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
$\Delta S=[7(214)+8(70)]-[329+11(205)]=2058-2584=-526$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$ $=-0.526$ kJ K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$.
$\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S=-4807-(298)(-0.526)=-4807+156.7=-4650$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
$\Delta G<0$, so the combustion is spontaneous at 298 K (the large negative $\Delta H$ outweighs the unfavourable entropy decrease).

questions.question: Diesel is a common fuel used in vehicles. Biodiesel, first commercially developed in 1991, is now readily available as an alternative fuel. A biofuels manufacturing facility, Shoalhaven Pty Ltd, in Nowra NSW, uses waste plant products from sugar and wheat processing and canola oil to produce biodiesel. Discuss advantages and disadvantages of producing and/or using biodiesel as a sustainable fuel for transport and describe THREE significant factors that may have been considered when building the Shoalhaven biofuels facility.
questions.answer:
**Advantages**
- Biodiesel is made from crops and waste plant material that can be regrown, so it is renewable, whereas fossil diesel is a finite resource.
- It produces fewer harmful emissions (less CO, particulates and sulfur compounds), and it can be regarded as close to carbon neutral because the $\text{CO}_2$ released on combustion was taken in by the plants as they grew.

**Disadvantages**
- It is often more expensive to produce than fossil diesel, and growing crops such as canola can use arable land and large amounts of water that could be used for food.
- It can corrode some metals and degrade some seals and is not suitable for all engines without modification, and it has a lower energy density than fossil diesel.

**Factors considered when building the Shoalhaven facility**
1. *Feedstock supply:* it was built near sugar, wheat and canola growing and processing regions so that waste plant products are available locally and transport costs and emissions are low.
2. *Transport and infrastructure:* access to roads, rail and the port at Nowra allows biodiesel to be distributed easily, and the existing industrial services (water, electricity) support the process, which needs large amounts of water and energy.
3. *Environmental, economic and social impact:* using waste products reduces competition with food production and landfill, creates local jobs, and the plant needs environmental approvals for waste, emissions and water use.
